summary: Discusses security issues with the way BGP spreads routing data. BGP has no internal mechanisms to protect against attacks that modify, delete, forge, or replay data, which could disrupt routing. The document does not cover security issues with packet forwarding. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4272 examines how outsiders and BGP peers can send false routing information or disrupt a BGP connection. It explains what TCP MD5 can protect and why a legitimate peer can still cause routing harm.

questions: what are the security vulnerabilities of bgp
what does tcp md5 protect in bgp
how can a bgp peer fake as path
subtitle: How forged or altered BGP routing information can disrupt networks.

tldr.problem: BGP has no built-in protection against routing messages that are changed, deleted, forged, or replayed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes attacks on BGP messages, path attributes, TCP, and supporting management functions, and discusses protections and remaining risks.
tldr.outcome: TCP MD5 can counter many attacks by outsiders, but it cannot prevent a legitimate peer from announcing false routing information.

today: RFC 4272 is an Informational document published in January 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the analysis is based on BGP as specified in RFC 4271.

sections.title: What BGP Security Must Protect
sections.content:
Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) exchanges routing information between autonomous systems. The RFC says BGP was designed without internal protection against deliberate or accidental errors in that information. An attacker may be an outsider or a legitimate BGP peer.

False routing data can remove reachability, send traffic along a poor or malicious path, cause loops, or overload routers. This document analyzes routing-data distribution. It does not analyze security of packet forwarding itself.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP routers share directions for reaching networks, but BGP does not verify that those directions are true. False directions can interrupt service or send traffic through an unintended network.

sections.title: Attacks and TCP MD5
sections.content:
BGP sends routing data in clear text and provides no replay protection. It also lacks built-in protection against message insertion, deletion, or modification, and it does not authenticate the other peer. Because BGP uses TCP, an outsider's ability to inject or remove messages is made harder by TCP sequence numbers, but is not eliminated.

BGP implementations must support the TCP MD5 mechanism described by the RFC. When used, it counters several outsider attacks, including message changes and man-in-the-middle attacks. It does not hide routing data, stop replay in all cases, or prevent a legitimate peer from sending false routes.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP MD5 can help confirm that messages came from an expected peer and were not changed in transit. It cannot make a dishonest peer tell the truth.

sections.title: Three Fundamental Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three gaps: BGP has no strong built-in protection for message integrity, freshness, or peer identity; it does not verify an AS's authority to announce network-layer reachability information (NLRI); and it does not verify the authenticity of announced path attributes.

A forged OPEN, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, or UPDATE may disrupt a connection. A false UPDATE can also change routing while the connection remains active. Attributes such as AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, and NLRI can be abused by a malicious peer; TCP MD5 does not prevent those insider announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP does not prove who sent a route, whether the route is fresh, or whether the sender is allowed to announce it. A connected peer can therefore send plausible but false route details.

sections.title: How UPDATE Fields Can Be Misused
sections.content:
An UPDATE message can withdraw routes, announce network-layer reachability information, and carry path attributes. A forged withdrawal can remove a route. A false AS_PATH can make a route more attractive or create a routing loop, while a false NEXT_HOP can misdirect traffic or make another AS carry it.

The RFC also discusses false origins, NLRI, and ATOMIC_AGGREGATE. MULTI_EXIT_DISC and LOCAL_PREF affect decisions within limited scopes, while AGGREGATOR is not used for routing decisions and is not identified as a vulnerability.
sections.plainLanguage: Route announcements contain several fields, and each can affect where traffic goes. False path, next-hop, or destination information can misdirect traffic or make a network unreachable.

sections.title: Residual Risk and Operational Protection
sections.content:
The RFC lists possible protections beyond TCP MD5 and IPsec: signing the originating AS, signing the origin and predecessor information, signing AS_PATH information, and filtering routes against a registry. It says filtering was used near some customer attachment points, while the other approaches remained controversial and were not in common use at the time of publication.

It also describes filtering packets at provider borders to protect internal addresses and BGP port 179. Management and configuration channels matter too, because they can trigger events that stop a BGP connection or change timers.
sections.plainLanguage: Cryptographic checks do not stop false information from a trusted peer. Route filtering and protected management access can reduce some risks, but the RFC describes limits to those measures.
